title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
text: This page reactivates the first-year linear algebra that Week 2 reuses. It does not introduce chains, boundary maps, cycle spaces or homology. Those are new TDA objects and belong in Week 2.

title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
text:
Scalars and fields
A scalar is a number used to scale a vector. A field is an arithmetic system in which addition, subtraction and multiplication are available, and division is available by every nonzero scalar. The familiar algebraic rules hold.
The rational numbers \(\mathbb Q\), real numbers \(\mathbb R\) and complex numbers \(\mathbb C\) are fields. The integers \(\mathbb Z\) are not a field because, for example, 2 has no multiplicative inverse that is also an integer.
A vector space is always defined over a specified field. Writing \(V=\mathbb R^n\) usually makes the field obvious. In a more abstract vector space, it must be stated.






NoteExample: why the choice of field cannot be omitted





Take the vector \(v=(1,0)\). If the surrounding vector space is \(\mathbb R^2\), then
\[
\sqrt2\,v=(\sqrt2,0)
\]
is another vector in the same space. Both \(1/2\) and \(\sqrt2\) are permitted scalars because they are real numbers.
Now consider the rational coordinate plane \(\mathbb Q^2\). The same written vector \(v=(1,0)\) belongs to this space, and \(\tfrac12v=(\tfrac12,0)\) remains in it. However, \(\sqrt2v=(\sqrt2,0)\) does not belong to \(\mathbb Q^2\) because \(\sqrt2\) is not rational. If we tried to call \(\mathbb Q^2\) a vector space over \(\mathbb R\), scalar multiplication would fail to stay inside the set. This violates a vector-space requirement called closure under scalar multiplication.
The field therefore specifies which coefficients are legal when vectors are scaled and combined. State vectors, regression coefficient vectors and perturbations are usually taken over \(\mathbb R\), so this choice is often present without being stated aloud. The phrase “vector space” is incomplete until its permitted scalars are known.




◆ TDA translation. Chains can be added without choosing a field. The coefficient system is still needed because it specifies what the coefficients are and how repeated simplices combine or cancel. Integer coefficients produce groups; field coefficients produce vector spaces. Week 2 begins with a field so that Gaussian elimination, rank and dimension apply directly. The coefficient discussion in Week 2 defines chains only after the underlying simplices have been introduced.


The coefficient field \(\mathbb F_2\)
The course begins with
\[
\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}.
\]
Arithmetic is modulo 2: only parity remains. Thus
\[
1+1=0,
\qquad
1-1=0,
\qquad
-1=1
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_2.
\]
This does not change ordinary integer arithmetic. It says that two occurrences have even parity, represented by 0 in this two-element field.
Algebraically, \(\mathbb F_2\) is the quotient \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\): all even integers form the class represented by 0, and all odd integers form the class represented by 1. The notation “modulo 2” means that integers differing by a multiple of 2 are deliberately treated as equivalent. The quotient interpretation is developed again with angles below.






NoteExample: parity as a toggle





Let 0 mean off and 1 mean on. Adding 1 toggles the state. Starting at 0, one toggle gives 1 and a second gives 0. The calculation \(1+1=0\) records this parity rule.





Other coefficient choices
The coefficient field determines which combinations and cancellations homology can distinguish. Common choices include:








Coefficients
What the arithmetic permits
When the choice may be sensible




\(\mathbb F_2\)
Binary coefficients and parity cancellation; orientation signs disappear.
A fast, transparent first analysis of components, loops or voids when orientation and torsion are not the question.


\(\mathbb F_p\) for an odd prime \(p\)
Arithmetic modulo \(p\), with signs and more than two coefficient values retained.
Comparing prime-dependent behaviour or probing torsion that may be visible at a particular prime.


\(\mathbb Q\)
Exact rational coefficients and ordinary signs, but no finite-field torsion.
Orientation-sensitive calculations when exact field arithmetic is useful and torsion is not required.


\(\mathbb R\)
Real coefficients and ordinary signs.
Compatibility with real-valued linear algebra or downstream numerical summaries, although it gives the same Betti numbers as \(\mathbb Q\) for finite simplicial complexes.


\(\mathbb C\)
Complex coefficients.
Problems carrying a natural complex-linear structure; it is uncommon as a default for ordinary TDA homology.



Integer coefficients \(\mathbb Z\) are also important, particularly when torsion and orientation matter, but \(\mathbb Z\) is not a field. The resulting homology objects are abelian groups rather than vector spaces, so rank alone no longer records all their structure. The system \(\mathbb F_p\) is a field only when \(p\) is prime. For example, arithmetic modulo 4 is not a field because the nonzero element 2 has no multiplicative inverse modulo 4.

◆ TDA translation. \(\mathbb F_2\) is a common TDA default because orientation signs disappear, coefficients are binary, reduction is exact, and binary columns can often be stored and reduced efficiently. Many first analyses ask whether components, loops or voids occur without requiring orientation-sensitive information.
This is convenience, not neutrality. Other fields can produce different homology. For example, the real projective plane has a one-dimensional first homology over \(\mathbb F_2\) but zero-dimensional first homology over \(\mathbb Q\). Week 2 uses \(\mathbb F_2\) transparently; an application concerned with orientation or torsion should choose or compare coefficients deliberately.
The coefficient field changes the algebraic lens, not the input representation. “The Betti number” should therefore mean the Betti number over a stated field.

title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
text:
Vectors, bases and coordinate columns
A vector space is a collection of objects that can be added and multiplied by scalars from a specified field. The span of vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) is the set of all their linear combinations:
\[
\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}
=
\left\{a_1v_1+\cdots+a_kv_k:
a_1,\ldots,a_k\text{ are scalars}\right\}.
\]
It is the smallest vector subspace containing those vectors. A basis is a collection of independent vectors whose span is the whole vector space. Every vector then has a unique linear combination of those basis vectors. The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the number of vectors in any basis for that space.
Order is not part of the abstract idea of a basis. It becomes relevant when coefficients are written as a coordinate tuple or placed into matrix rows and columns. For example, relative to the same two basis vectors \(b_1,b_2\), the coefficients \(2b_1+5b_2\) are written \((2,5)^T\) if the order is \((b_1,b_2)\) and \((5,2)^T\) if the order is \((b_2,b_1)\). The vector has not changed; only the bookkeeping order has.
Different bases of the same finite-dimensional vector space contain the same number of vectors, but they are not identical descriptions. Coordinates and matrices generally change with the basis. An invertible change-of-basis matrix translates between them, so no basis is intrinsically the only correct one. Some bases are more useful because they align with coordinates, eigenvectors, modes, sparsity or the objects in a computation.
A vector and its coordinate column are related but not identical:

the vector is the underlying object in the vector space;
the coordinate column records its coefficients relative to a selected basis and a stated order of that basis.

Changing the basis can change the coordinate column without changing the vector.






NoteExample: one vector in two bases





Use \(\mathbb R^2\) with its standard Cartesian coordinate system. Its standard basis vectors point along the horizontal and vertical coordinate axes:
\[
e_1=(1,0),\qquad e_2=(0,1).
\]
The vector \(v=3e_1+e_2\) has standard coordinate column
\[
[v]_{(e_1,e_2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Now use the basis
\[
b_1=(1,1),\qquad b_2=(1,-1).
\]
Since \(v=2b_1+b_2\), its coordinate column is
\[
[v]_{(b_1,b_2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The vector has not changed; its numerical description has.




Dynamical systems translation. A physical perturbation is an underlying vector. Its coordinates may be expressed in measured variables, an eigenvector basis or modal coordinates. Changing basis changes the numbers used to describe the perturbation, not the perturbation itself.


◆ TDA translation. Week 2 introduces new vector spaces whose basis elements happen to be vertices, edges or higher-dimensional simplices. Only there will a vector in such a space be named a chain. The Week 2 notes and lecture walkthrough make that translation explicit.


◇ Object check. At this point the objects are an ordinary vector space \(V\), a basis \(B\) and a vector \(v\in V\). To interpret the entries of the coordinate column \([v]_B\), the basis vectors must also be put in a stated order.

title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
text:
Linear maps and matrices
A linear map \(T:V\to W\) satisfies
\[
T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v),
\qquad
T(av)=aT(v).
\]
After bases \(B\) for \(V\) and \(C\) for \(W\) have been chosen and ordered, a matrix represents the map. It may be written
\[
A=[T]_{C\leftarrow B}.
\]
The objects have different roles:

\(T\) is the underlying linear map, independent of coordinates;
\(A\) is the numerical matrix representing \(T\) in the chosen input basis \(B\) and output basis \(C\).

Their relationship is
\[
[T(v)]_C=A[v]_B.
\]
Changing either basis can change \(A\) without changing \(T\). Each matrix column is the coordinate column of the output produced by one input basis vector.
The familiar \(2\times2\) format is
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b\\
c&d
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\x_2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
with
\[
Ax=
\begin{pmatrix}
ax_1+bx_2\\
cx_1+dx_2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
In standard Cartesian bases, it is common to identify vectors with their coordinate columns and write \(A=[T]\). The two columns then record
\[
[T(e_1)]=\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
[T(e_2)]=\begin{pmatrix}b\\d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The two rows determine the first and second output coordinates.






NoteExample: reading a 2 by 2 matrix by columns





Let \(T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) have the following matrix \(A=[T]\) in the standard Cartesian bases:
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
2&2
\end{pmatrix}
\]
in the standard basis. Its columns say
\[
T(e_1)=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T(e_2)=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Linearity then determines \(T\) on every input. For example,
\[
T\!\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=2T(e_1)-T(e_2)
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}.
\]




Dynamical systems translation. A Jacobian or linearised flow is the coordinate representation of how small perturbations are transported. The underlying linear map is the bigger-picture object; a particular matrix is its description after state variables and bases have been chosen. Reading columns asks how the chosen basis perturbations evolve, while changing coordinates changes the matrix without changing the underlying linear action.


◆ TDA translation. Week 2 first defines two new vector spaces and then defines a boundary map between them. In that setting, the boundary map is the analogue of \(T\). The simplices supply natural bases; ordering those simplices determines which simplex belongs to each row and column of the boundary matrix \(A=[T]_{C\leftarrow B}\). Each matrix column is then the coordinate representation of what the boundary map does to one basis simplex. Follow this construction in the Week 2 boundary-map development.

title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
text:
Kernel, image, rank and nullity
For a linear map \(T:V\to W\), the kernel is
\[
\ker T=\{v\in V:T(v)=0\}.
\]
It contains the input directions erased by the map. The image is
\[
\operatorname{im}T=\{T(v):v\in V\}.
\]
It contains the output directions the map can produce.
The dimension of the kernel counts the independent input directions that are collapsed to zero. This number is the nullity:
\[
\operatorname{nullity}T=\dim(\ker T).
\]
The dimension of the image counts the independent output directions that the map can produce. This number is the rank:
\[
\operatorname{rank}T=\dim(\operatorname{im}T).
\]
The rank-nullity theorem states that, for finite-dimensional \(V\),
\[
\dim V=\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T.
\]
The intuition is an accounting of input degrees of freedom. After a suitable basis is chosen, some independent input directions survive as independent output directions and the remaining independent directions lie in the kernel. Rank-nullity says that none of the input dimensions are unaccounted for.






NoteExample: kernel, image and rank of one matrix





For
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
2&2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
solving \(Ax=0\) gives
\[
x=t
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\ker A=\operatorname{span}\!\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\right\}.
\]
The two columns are identical, so every output is a multiple of \((1,2)^T\):
\[
\operatorname{im}A=\operatorname{span}\!\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, the map acts as
\[
T(x_1,x_2)=
\bigl(x_1+x_2,\,2(x_1+x_2)\bigr).
\]
It compresses the whole Cartesian plane onto the line spanned by \((1,2)\). Moving in the input direction \((1,-1)\) changes \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by equal and opposite amounts, so their sum stays fixed and the output does not change. That direction is erased and spans the kernel.
There is one independent output direction, so the rank is 1. There is one independent erased input direction, so the nullity is 1. The two-dimensional input is therefore accounted for by
\[
2=1+1.
\]




Dynamical systems translation. Kernel and image describe information flow more generally. The kernel contains distinctions in the input that the map cannot transmit; the image is the set of output directions the map can realise. Rank measures how many independent directions survive the map, while nullity measures how many independent directions are lost. This interpretation applies to observation operators, linearisations, reduced models and control maps, not only to a particular matrix calculation.


◆ TDA translation. Week 2 applies kernel and image to adjacent boundary maps. The kernel will be given the new name cycle space, and an adjacent image will be given the new name boundary space. Homology then compares them. Those definitions and the outline-versus-filled triangle belong in Week 2, not in this refresher.

title: Before Week 2: Algebra survival guide
section: Quotients: one idea that may be less familiar
text:
Quotients: one idea that may be less familiar
A quotient treats an agreed kind of difference as irrelevant. This is not ordinary division. If an equivalence relation declares \(v\sim w\), the quotient collects all equivalent objects into one class.






NoteExample: angles modulo one full turn





Angles provide a quotient that is used routinely without being named as one. The angles
\[
0,\qquad 2\pi,\qquad -2\pi,\qquad 4\pi
\]
are different real numbers but represent the same direction. More generally,
\[
\theta\sim\phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\theta-\phi=2\pi k
\text{ for some }k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Working “modulo \(2\pi\)” replaces every collection of angles differing by whole turns with one angle class. The quotient is written \(\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\) and represents the circle of directions.
In this algebraic sense, working modulo something is always quotienting by a stated equivalence: differences belonging to the specified subgroup are treated as irrelevant. Thus integers modulo \(n\) form the quotient \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\), where numbers differing by a multiple of \(n\) belong to the same class. In elementary arithmetic, “take the remainder” chooses a convenient representative of that class. The quotient is the full class, not merely the selected remainder. Informal phrases such as “modulo numerical error” are looser language and need not name a formal quotient.









NoteExample: identifying states related by a symmetry





Suppose a rotationally symmetric system treats states \(x\) and \(R_\theta x\) as equivalent for every rotation \(R_\theta\). The quotient does not claim those state vectors are identical. It constructs a reduced description in which their rotational difference is deliberately ignored.




Dynamical systems translation. Symmetry reduction is a quotient construction. Many full states can correspond to one reduced state because the chosen symmetry direction is no longer distinguished.


◆ TDA translation. Week 2 introduces homology as a quotient only after cycles and boundaries have been defined. Its interpretation is that cycles differing by an available boundary represent the same class. Follow that argument in the Week 2 triangle example; it is new TDA content rather than assumed first-year algebra.

text:
This is the live worked example, built around the outline and filled triangle, square loop and hollow tetrahedron. It follows the conceptual argument of the slides through prediction, reveal and interpretation. It is not intended as a line-by-line answer key to the participant practical.
Resource boundary. The reference notes define the objects and explain the algebra. The slides organise the live argument. This notebook works every central example to completion. The participant practical retains the same small complexes but leaves matrix reading, checks and interpretation to students.
Lecture map. Begin with the same 1-skeleton drawn as an outline and filled triangle. Reveal the chain spaces and boundary matrices only after predictions. Compare the square loop, then lift the argument by one dimension with the hollow and solid tetrahedron.
This practical makes the algebra visible before any TDA library is used. We will move through
\[K \longrightarrow C_p(K;\mathbb F_2) \xrightarrow{\partial_p} C_{p-1}(K;\mathbb F_2)
\longrightarrow Z_p/B_p = H_p(K;\mathbb F_2).\]
The examples are deliberately small: an outline triangle, a filled triangle, a square loop and a hollow tetrahedron.
◇ Object check. The simplicial complex \(K\) is a collection of simplices. The chain space \(C_p\) is a vector space whose chosen basis is the list of \(p\)-simplices. A matrix represents a boundary map only after those bases and their orders have been fixed.
Presenter route. Use the outline-to-filled triangle as the central reveal: the 1-skeleton stays fixed while \(C_2\), \(\partial_2\) and \(H_1\) change.
Prerequisite bridge. Use the algebra survival guide if basis, kernel, image, rank or quotient are unfamiliar.

title: Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
1. Observe: lecture demonstration
Presenter cue. Show the object before the calculation. Ask the room to separate what is given from what will be constructed.
The first three complexes are drawn below. The hollow tetrahedron is the union of its four triangular faces. It does not contain the solid tetrahedral 3-simplex.
Before computing, distinguish the visible drawing from the mathematical object. In particular, the outline and filled triangles have the same vertices and edges, hence the same 1-skeleton, but they are different simplicial complexes.


Code
positions_2d = {
    "outline triangle": {0:(0,0), 1:(1,0), 2:(0.5,0.87)},
    "filled triangle": {0:(0,0), 1:(1,0), 2:(0.5,0.87)},
    "square loop": {0:(0,0), 1:(1,0), 2:(1,1), 3:(0,1)},
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2))
for ax, (name, K) in zip(axes, list(complexes.items())[:3]):
    pos = positions_2d[name]
    if K.get(2):
        for face in K[2]:
            ax.fill(*zip(*(pos[v] for v in face)), alpha=0.25, color='tab:blue')
    for edge in K.get(1, []):
        ax.plot(*zip(*(pos[v] for v in edge)), color='black')
    for v, xy in pos.items():
        ax.scatter(*xy, s=80, zorder=3)
        ax.text(xy[0], xy[1] + 0.08, str(v), ha='center')
    ax.set_title(name)
    ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
plt.show()
print("The hollow tetrahedron contains four triangular faces but no 3-simplex.")

title: Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
2. Predict: lecture demonstration
Presenter cue. Pause here and collect at least two predictions before revealing any output.
Without running the homology calculations, complete this table. Count a connected component as an \(H_0\) class.










Complex
Expected \(\beta_0\)
Expected \(\beta_1\)
Expected \(\beta_2\)
Which simplex could fill the visible cycle?




Outline triangle






Filled triangle






Square loop






Hollow tetrahedron







Also predict whether adding the triangular 2-simplex to the outline triangle changes \(C_0\), \(C_1\), \(C_2\), or more than one of them.
Worked prediction. All four complexes are connected, so \(\beta_0=1\). The outline triangle and square loop each have one unfilled 1-cycle. The filled triangle has no nonzero higher-dimensional homology. The hollow tetrahedron has one 2-dimensional surface cycle. Thus the expected Betti vectors are \((1,1)\), \((1,0,0)\), \((1,1)\) and \((1,0,1)\). A 2-simplex fills each planar loop; a 3-simplex fills the tetrahedral surface.

title: Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
3. Implement: lecture demonstration
Reveal. Run one cell at a time. Name the domain, codomain, complex, module or summary before interpreting its values.
Run the setup cell. close_under_faces enforces downward closure. boundary_matrix creates the matrix of \(\partial_p\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): an entry is 1 when the row simplex is a codimension-one face of the column simplex.
Because \(-1=1\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), orientations and signs disappear. This is convenient, but it is a coefficient choice, not a property of homology in general.

A. Read a boundary matrix


Code
d1_outline = boundary_matrix(outline_triangle, 1)
print('rows, basis C_0:', outline_triangle[0])
print('columns, basis C_1:', outline_triangle[1])
print(d1_outline)
triangle_edge_cycle = np.ones(3, dtype=np.uint8)
print('boundary of all three edges:', (d1_outline @ triangle_edge_cycle) % 2)


The map is \(\partial_1:C_1\to C_0\). Each column contains the two endpoints of its edge. Adding all columns gives zero because every vertex occurs twice. The edge sum is therefore in \(Z_1\).


B. Check that boundaries are cycles


Code
d1_filled = boundary_matrix(filled_triangle, 1)
d2_filled = boundary_matrix(filled_triangle, 2)
print('(∂_1 ∂_2) =')
print((d1_filled @ d2_filled) % 2)
for name, K in complexes.items():
    print(name, check_boundary_squared(K))


The zero product states that the boundary of the triangular face has no boundary. More generally, \(\partial_p\partial_{p+1}=0\), so every vector in \(\operatorname{im}\partial_{p+1}=B_p\) lies in \(\ker\partial_p=Z_p\).


C. Compute homology dimensions


Code
report('outline triangle', outline_triangle)
report('square loop', square_loop)


Both are connected and have one independent edge cycle with no 2-chain available to bound it. Their visible geometry differs, but their Betti numbers over \(\mathbb F_2\) agree.

title: Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
4. Compare: lecture demonstration


Code
report('outline triangle', outline_triangle)
report('filled triangle', filled_triangle)


Adding the face leaves \(C_0\), \(C_1\) and \(\partial_1\) unchanged. It creates a one-dimensional \(C_2\) and a nonzero \(\partial_2\). The old edge cycle remains in \(Z_1\), but it is now also in \(B_1\), so its class is zero in \(H_1=Z_1/B_1\). This is why the complex must not be confused with its 1-skeleton.

The hollow tetrahedron


Code
faces = hollow_tetrahedron[2]
hollow_surface = np.ones(len(faces), dtype=np.uint8)
d2_hollow = boundary_matrix(hollow_tetrahedron, 2)
print('boundary of the four-face surface:', (d2_hollow @ hollow_surface) % 2)
report('hollow tetrahedron', hollow_tetrahedron)
solid_tetrahedron = close_under_faces([(0, 1, 2, 3)])
report('solid tetrahedron', solid_tetrahedron)
print('boundary of its 3-simplex:', boundary_matrix(solid_tetrahedron, 3).ravel())


Every edge of the hollow surface occurs in two faces, so the face sum is a 2-cycle. With no 3-simplex, \(B_2=0\) and \(\beta_2=1\). Adding the solid tetrahedron creates \(C_3\cong\mathbb F_2\); its boundary is exactly the four-face cycle, which becomes zero in \(H_2\).


D. Use Euler characteristic as a cross-check
For a finite complex,
\[\chi(K)=\sum_p(-1)^p\dim C_p=\sum_p(-1)^p\beta_p.\]
Check both sides for all four examples. Explain why agreement is useful but does not prove that every individual Betti number is correct.


Code
def euler_from_simplices(K):
    return sum((-1)**p * len(K.get(p, [])) for p in K)

def euler_from_betti(K):
    return sum((-1)**p * row[-1] for p, row in enumerate(homology_table(K)))

for name, K in complexes.items():
    left = euler_from_simplices(K)
    right = euler_from_betti(K)
    print(f"{name}: simplex count gives {left}; Betti numbers give {right}")
    assert left == right


Agreement checks the alternating total of the computed dimensions. It cannot locate an error by degree: simultaneous errors in adjacent Betti numbers can cancel in the alternating sum. Boundary ranks and \(\partial^2=0\) must still be checked directly.


Quotient checkpoint: worked
In the filled triangle, \(z-0=z=\partial_2(012)\in B_1\), so \(z\sim0\) and \([z]=[0]\). More generally, if \(z'-z\) is the boundary of an available two-chain, then \(z'\sim z\) and both cycles represent the same homology class.
A homology class is one equivalence class containing many cycle representatives. The quotient forgets changes produced by adding boundaries.

title: Week 2 lecture walkthrough: simplices, boundary maps and homology over \(\mathbb F_2\)
text:
5. Interpret: lecture demonstration
Presenter close. Ask what the example supports, what information was discarded and which stronger claim would be unjustified.

The outline cycle is not a boundary because \(C_2=0\). In the filled triangle the same chain equals the boundary of the 2-simplex.
A homology class is an equivalence class of cycles modulo boundaries. A drawn loop is only one possible representative.
The tetrahedral 3-simplex fills the hollow tetrahedron’s \(H_2\) class.
The matrix arithmetic, cancellation of duplicate faces, and omission of orientation signs here use \(\mathbb F_2\). The definitions of cycles, boundaries and quotient homology persist with other coefficients, but the algebra can change.
Filling a 3-clique asserts that three pairwise relations constitute a higher-order unit. That is a modelling decision, not information contained in the graph alone.

† Qualification. These calculations describe the topology of the constructed simplicial complex. Whether that complex faithfully represents a dynamical system is a separate scientific and modelling question.

title: Applied glossary
text:
Objects and representations









Mathematical term
Precise meaning
Applied or intuitive translation
Interpretation caution




Topological space
A set equipped with open sets satisfying the topology axioms.
A specification of which points count as locally near one another, without requiring numerical distance.
“Topology” is not a generic synonym for shape or network layout.


Homeomorphism
A bijection whose forward and inverse maps are continuous.
A reversible deformation that preserves topological structure.
The rubber-sheet metaphor is only an intuition, and finite samples are not automatically homeomorphic to latent continuous spaces.


Homotopy equivalence
Maps in both directions whose composites are homotopic to the corresponding identity maps.
Two spaces retain the same broad continuous shape after contractible detail is ignored.
It is weaker than homeomorphism and does not preserve metric geometry.


Topological invariant
A quantity or algebraic object unchanged under homeomorphism.
A shape descriptor designed to ignore coordinates and reversible deformation.
In data analysis it is computed on a constructed representation, not directly on an unknown physical system.


Constructed representation
A mathematical object built from observations and modelling choices.
The point cloud, graph, image complex or embedding through which the system is analysed.
It can amplify, erase or invent apparent organisation relative to the scientific object.


Metric
A distance function satisfying non-negativity, identity, symmetry and the triangle inequality.
The rule that decides which observations are similar enough to interact first.
A convenient metric may be scientifically inappropriate.


Point cloud
A finite subset of a metric space.
A collection of sampled states or observations represented as points.
It is a representation of the system, not automatically the system or attractor itself.


Geometric descriptor
A quantity or representation measuring a specified metric or coordinate property of a geometric object.
One deliberately chosen answer to “what makes these shapes look different?”, such as spacing, area, direction or curvature.
No short list of descriptors is a complete definition of shape; inspect what each retains and discards.


Convex hull
The smallest convex set containing a specified set of points.
A tight elastic band placed around the outermost observations.
It records the outer envelope but cannot detect internal gaps, density or concavity.


Anisotropy
Dependence of measured properties on direction.
Evidence that a cloud stretches or organises more strongly along some directions than others.
A single anisotropy ratio can miss curvature, multiple branches and local changes in direction.


Geometric simplex
The convex hull of affinely independent vertices.
A filled-in building block: point, segment, triangle, tetrahedron.
A drawn triangle and three edges do not specify whether the face is filled.


Abstract simplex
A finite set of vertices.
A recorded multiway relation among the listed vertices.
It need not have physical extent or a unique embedding.


Simplicial complex
A collection of simplices closed under taking faces.
A consistent catalogue of relations at every included order.
Its 1-skeleton does not determine its higher-dimensional simplices.


Geometric realisation \(|K|\)
A topological space obtained by realising and gluing the simplices of \(K\).
A spatial version of the abstract incidence data.
The realisation is not necessarily the observed physical object.


1-skeleton
All vertices and edges of a complex.
The network visible after discarding filled triangles and higher relations.
Homology of the graph may differ from homology of the full complex.


Clique complex
The complex containing a simplex for every clique of a graph.
Treat every mutually pairwise-connected group as one higher-order unit.
Clique filling is a modelling assumption about higher-order coherence.


Graph cycle rank
For a finite undirected graph, \(E-V+C\), the dimension of its cycle space over a field.
The number of independent network loops before any higher-dimensional filling is added.
It is not generally \(H_1\) of the clique complex because triangles and higher simplices can fill graph cycles.

title: Applied glossary
text:
Homology as linear algebra









Mathematical term
Precise meaning
Applied or intuitive translation
Interpretation caution




Basis
A linearly independent spanning set giving every vector unique coordinates.
The agreed list of elementary pieces used to record a combination.
Coordinates depend on the selected basis even when the vector does not.


Span
All linear combinations of a specified set of vectors.
Everything that can be assembled from the available building blocks.
A long generating list may contain redundant vectors.


Kernel
For \(T:V\to W\), the subspace \(\{v:T(v)=0\}\).
Input combinations whose effects cancel completely under the map.
Being in a kernel is relative to a particular map.


Image
For \(T:V\to W\), the subspace \(\{T(v):v\in V\}\).
Output patterns that the available inputs can actually produce.
The image need not equal the full codomain.


Rank
The dimension of the image of a linear map.
The number of independent output directions produced by the map.
Matrix rank is basis-independent, though the matrix entries are not.


Nullity
The dimension of the kernel of a linear map.
The number of independent input directions erased by the map.
A large nullity has meaning only after the domain and map are named.


Quotient vector space \(V/W\)
Equivalence classes under \(v\sim v'\) when \(v-v'\in W\).
Treat differences lying in \(W\) as irrelevant or already accounted for.
The slash is not numerical division, and a class has many representatives.


Equivalence class \([v]\)
All elements equivalent to \(v\) under a specified relation.
Every representation treated as the same after the agreed differences are ignored.
A displayed representative is not canonical unless additional structure selects it.


Coefficient field
The field used for chain coefficients, here usually \(\mathbb F_2\).
The arithmetic system used to combine and cancel building blocks.
Features can depend on coefficients, especially in the presence of torsion.


Chain space \(C_p\)
The vector space freely generated by the \(p\)-simplices.
All formal selections or combinations of \(p\)-dimensional pieces.
A chain is algebraic bookkeeping, not necessarily one connected geometric object.


Boundary map \(\partial_p\)
The linear map sending each \(p\)-simplex to the signed sum of its faces.
A rule extracting the exposed lower-dimensional boundary of a collection of pieces.
Over \(\mathbb F_2\) signs vanish; over other coefficients orientation matters.


Cycle \(Z_p\)
A chain in \(\ker\partial_p\).
A closed algebraic pattern with no remaining boundary.
A cycle need not represent a nonzero hole; it may itself be a boundary.


Boundary \(B_p\)
A chain in \(\operatorname{im}\partial_{p+1}\).
A closed pattern already filled by something one dimension higher.
“Boundary” here is algebraic, not merely the visible edge of a plotted region.


Homology \(H_p\)
The quotient \(Z_p/B_p\).
Closed patterns counted only after filled or equivalent versions are identified.
A class is an equivalence class of cycles, not a privileged loop.


Betti number \(\beta_p\)
The dimension of \(H_p\) over the chosen field.
The number of independent \(p\)-dimensional topological degrees of freedom.
It is a count at one object or scale and contains no feature identity.


Euler characteristic \(\chi\)
The alternating sum of simplex counts, equivalently Betti numbers for a finite complex.
A compact accounting checksum for the complex.
Different homology can share the same Euler characteristic.

title: Applied glossary
text:
Filtrations and persistence









Mathematical term
Precise meaning
Applied or intuitive translation
Interpretation caution




Filtration
A nested family \(K_a\subseteq K_b\) for \(a\leq b\).
A controlled sweep through a modelling threshold.
The parameter is not automatically physical time.


Filtration function
A face-monotone value assigned to every simplex.
The rule deciding when each relation becomes available.
Birth inherits meaning from this rule, not from topology alone.


Čech complex
The nerve of equal-radius balls centred on a point cloud.
Record groups whose neighbourhoods share a genuinely common point.
Joint intersection is stronger than pairwise intersection.


Vietoris–Rips complex
The clique complex on pairs below a distance threshold.
Infer higher-order groups from pairwise proximity.
Check whether the parameter denotes radius or pairwise-distance threshold.


Inclusion-induced map
The map \(H_p(K_a)\to H_p(K_b)\) induced by \(K_a\hookrightarrow K_b\).
The rule describing what an earlier feature becomes after more simplices are added.
The map need not be injective; an old class can map to zero.


Functor
A rule sending objects to objects and maps to maps while preserving identities and composition.
A consistent translation that retains both the states and how one state maps to another.
The word adds no new empirical information; it records a structural compatibility.


Persistence module
Vector spaces \(H_p(K_a)\) together with all compatible maps across scale.
Homology with its cross-scale memory retained.
A sequence of Betti numbers is not a persistence module.


Birth
The first parameter at which a class appears in the module.
The threshold where a new independent organisation becomes detectable.
It is construction-dependent and may arise from sampling or ties.


Death
The parameter where a class merges into an older class or becomes a boundary.
The threshold where that independent organisation is no longer distinguishable.
The underlying chain may still exist after its class dies.


Persistence
Death minus birth for a finite interval.
The range of thresholds over which a class remains distinguishable.
Long persistence is not automatically scientific importance.


Interval module
A module equal to the field on one interval and zero elsewhere.
One idealised feature that is alive over one parameter range.
The full module is usually a direct sum of many intervals.


Barcode
The multiset of intervals in an interval decomposition.
A timeline-like display of feature lifetimes across scale.
Classification by barcodes needs suitable one-parameter finiteness or tameness assumptions.


Persistence diagram
Birth-death points encoding the same interval data.
A scatter plot of when features appear and disappear.
Distance from the diagonal measures persistence, not truth or usefulness.


Representative cycle
A cycle chosen from a homology class.
One concrete loop or void boundary used to localise an abstract feature.
The choice is generally not unique, so its precise location should not be treated as canonical.


Essential class
A class with no finite death in the available filtration.
Structure that remains after the sweep reaches its endpoint.
It may be genuinely global or merely censored by a truncated parameter range.


Stability
A theorem bounding diagram change by an appropriate change in input or filtration.
Small permitted perturbations cannot arbitrarily move the persistence output.
Stability does not imply interpretability, significance or predictive value.

title: Applied glossary
text:
Dynamic data









Mathematical term
Precise meaning
Applied or intuitive translation
Interpretation caution




Repeated persistence
Separate static persistence computations at successive times or windows.
A movie of barcode summaries.
Similar-looking bars are not automatically the same tracked feature.


Vineyard
Trajectories of persistence-diagram points under a changing function.
Feature summaries traced continuously as data evolve.
Matching diagram points is additional structure beyond repeated diagrams.


Zigzag persistence
Persistence for diagrams whose maps may point forward or backward.
Track structure when observations or complexes can be added and removed.
It solves a different problem from an ordinary increasing filtration.


Multiparameter persistence
A module indexed by a partial order with two or more parameters.
Retain several genuine modelling axes without collapsing them prematurely.
There is generally no complete barcode classification analogous to the one-parameter case.


Simplex tree
A data structure storing simplices, faces and filtration values in a prefix tree.
A computational index for querying and updating a filtered complex.
It is a representation in software, not a new topological object.


Cubical complex
A complex built from vertices, edges, pixels, voxels and higher-dimensional cubes.
A topology-ready representation of gridded images, fields or volumes.
Cell-value conventions and sublevel direction determine birth meaning.


Lower-star filtration
A filtration assigning each simplex the maximum value on its vertices.
Activate a relation when its highest-valued required vertex becomes available.
Negating values changes a low-feature question into a high-feature question.


Bottleneck distance
The minimum possible maximum matching cost between diagrams, allowing diagonal matches.
The size of the single worst discrepancy after optimal matching.
It can ignore the accumulated effect of many smaller changes.


Wasserstein distance
An optimal matching cost that aggregates powered pointwise costs.
Total diagram discrepancy rather than only the worst match.
Its value depends on the order, ground metric and treatment of diagonal matches.


Betti curve
The function counting intervals alive at each filtration value.
A multiscale feature-count profile.
It discards interval identity and can map different diagrams to the same curve.


Persistence image
A weighted, smoothed rasterisation of diagram points.
A fixed-length feature array for statistics or machine learning.
Resolution, smoothing and weighting are modelling parameters.


Persistence entropy
Shannon entropy of normalised interval lengths, usually for finite intervals.
A scalar describing how evenly persistence is distributed across features.
It discards birth locations and feature identity, and conventions for essential or zero-length intervals matter.


Mapper
A graph or simplicial complex built from overlapping bins of a filter function and clusters within their inverse images.
A compressed atlas of how observations organise along a chosen lens.
Its topology depends on the filter, cover and clustering, and it is not a persistence diagram.


Null model
A probability model representing structure expected without the target mechanism.
The comparison world against which “unusual” is defined.
An easy-to-simulate null may preserve the wrong properties.


Surrogate data
Synthetic or transformed observations generated under a null while preserving selected features.
A controlled negative comparison passed through the same pipeline.
Validity depends on what is preserved, destroyed and exchangeable.


CROCKER-style plot
A display of Betti number or rank across physical time and filtration scale.
A heat map of how multiscale topological counts evolve.
It summarises repeated diagrams and does not track class identity.


Physical time \(t\)
The external index describing when a system is observed.
Clock time, trial progress or window position.
It must not be confused with filtration scale.


Filtration scale \(\varepsilon\)
The ordered threshold within one persistence calculation.
The resolution or relation-strength dial used to construct topology.
It is not necessarily a physical unit unless the construction supports that interpretation.


Feature tracking
An explicit correspondence assigning identity to features across an external index.
Saying which evolving feature is the continuation of which earlier feature.
Nearest diagram points or similar lifetimes do not automatically establish identity.


Interleaving
Compatible shifted maps between persistence modules.
A controlled way to compare modules while allowing parameter tolerance.
A small interleaving distance does not uniquely match generators.


Vineyard module
A time-indexed family of persistence modules with coherent transport maps.
Vines plus the algebra describing how feature directions mix through time.
It is richer than a vineyard and requires additional structure to estimate.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
Story
Week 2 moves from qualitative shape to a combinatorial object on which topology can be computed. The central message is that a simplicial complex is the finite bookkeeping device that lets topology become linear algebra. The complex is treated as already chosen. The aim is to understand what homology computes once \(K\) has been chosen.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
Mathematics to introduce
Geometric simplex: convex hull of \(p+1\) affinely independent points.
Abstract simplex: a set of \(p+1\) vertices.
\[\sigma\in K,\ \tau\subseteq\sigma\Longrightarrow\tau\in K.\]
The notebooks use abstract complexes: incidence matters; coordinates do not.
◇ Object check. At this stage, \(K\) is the topological/combinatorial object. The vector spaces come next: one vector space \(C_p(K;\mathbb F)\) for the \(p\)-simplices in each dimension.

\[
\cdots\to C_2(K;\mathbb F_2)
\xrightarrow{\partial_2}C_1(K;\mathbb F_2)
\xrightarrow{\partial_1}C_0(K;\mathbb F_2)\to0
\]
\[\partial_{p-1}\partial_p=0.\]
Therefore
\[B_p=\operatorname{im}\partial_{p+1}\subseteq
Z_p=\ker\partial_p.\]

\[C_2=0,\qquad z=e_{01}+e_{12}+e_{02}\in Z_1\setminus B_1.\]
Filled triangle:
\[C_2=\langle [012]\rangle,\qquad z=\partial_2[012]\in B_1.\]
The cycle remains. Its class in \(Z_1/B_1\) changes.

▶ Likely sticking point. A simplicial complex is not determined by its drawing or its 1-skeleton. The triangular 2-simplex is extra data.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
Boundary maps become matrices
Choose simplex bases and fix their order. Each column of \([\partial_p]\) is the boundary of one \(p\)-simplex.
Over \(\mathbb F_2\):
\[[\partial_{p-1}][\partial_p]=0,
\qquad
\beta_p=\dim C_p-\operatorname{rank}\partial_p-
\operatorname{rank}\partial_{p+1}.\]

◇ Object check. The matrix is a representation of a linear map. Its rows and columns only make sense after the chain-space bases are named.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
Examples to compute
Use a square loop as the simplest visible \(H_1\) class and a hollow tetrahedron as a first \(H_2\) example. Ask explicitly which chains are cycles, which cycles are boundaries, and which distinctions survive in the quotient.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
Two computational checks
\[\beta_p=\dim C_p-\operatorname{rank}\partial_p-
\operatorname{rank}\partial_{p+1}.\]
\[\chi(K)=\sum_p(-1)^p\dim C_p
=\sum_p(-1)^p\beta_p.\]
Euler characteristic is a check, not a replacement for homology.

title: Week 2: Simplicial complexes and homology: building a computable hole-counter
text:
DP relevance
Graphs enter as the simplest data-derived complexes. An interaction graph can be treated as a one-dimensional simplicial complex, with vertices and edges only. This supports component and graph-cycle homology. To study higher-dimensional topology, the graph must be promoted to another object, such as a clique complex. That promotion is a modelling assumption: pairwise mutual interaction is being treated as evidence of a higher-order collective unit.

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
Story
Week 8 should be organised by problem type rather than by a list of advanced methods. The aim is to teach method selection: what breaks in ordinary persistence, and which tool responds to that break?
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
Case 1: complexes only grow
If complexes only grow, ordinary one-parameter persistence is the natural tool. This is the clean barcode setting. The inclusion maps all point in the same direction: \[K_0\subseteq K_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq K_n.\]
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
Case 2: complexes grow and shrink
If complexes grow and shrink, zigzag persistence is the natural extension. Instead of all maps pointing in one direction, the diagram can zigzag: \[K_0\to K_1 \leftarrow K_2 \to K_3 \leftarrow \cdots.\] Zigzag persistence is designed for insertions and deletions of simplices. It is mathematically appropriate for non-monotone sequences, but it can be computationally and interpretively heavy.

Standard persistence tracks features that survive as a space grows. Zigzag persistence tracks features that survive as a space changes.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Case 3: there is more than one genuine parameter
text:
Case 3: there is more than one genuine parameter
If scale and time, scale and density, or another pair of parameters are both genuine, then multiparameter persistence is the relevant framework. The warning is essential: the clean barcode decomposition of one-parameter persistence does not carry over in the same way. Multiparameter persistence may be the right mathematical object even when a practical analysis later uses lower-dimensional summaries.
† Qualification. The presence of two named variables does not by itself decide the framework. The question is whether they form one partial order to be analysed jointly, or whether one parameter indexes a controlled family of ordinary persistence modules with additional transport data.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Case 4: a fixed complex has a smoothly changing filtration
text:
Case 4: a fixed complex has a smoothly changing filtration
Vineyards apply when there is a fixed simplicial complex \(K\) and a time-dependent filtration function \[f_t:K\to\mathbb{R}.\] There are now two distinct parameters: \[\underbrace{t}_{\text{external or physical time}},
\qquad
\underbrace{a}_{\text{filtration height or scale}}.\] At each fixed time \(t\), the sublevel filtration of \(f_t\) produces an ordinary persistence module \[V_t(a)=H_p(K_{t,a};\mathbb F)\] and a persistence diagram \(D_t\). A vineyard tracks how the birth–death points of \(D_t\) move as \(t\) varies. Each tracked curve is a vine.
The useful teaching picture is a landscape whose height function changes over time. Ordinary persistence studies flooding one fixed landscape. A vineyard studies what happens when the landscape itself slowly morphs.
Vineyards assume controlled change. The set of simplices is fixed, filtration values vary continuously, and changes in the filtration order occur through adjacent swaps. Between swaps, persistence pairings remain fixed and vines move linearly or smoothly. At a swap, the reduced boundary matrix is updated locally rather than recomputed from scratch.
† Qualification. A vineyard is a geometric record of moving birth–death points. It does not automatically retain the full linear maps connecting the persistence modules at different times.

A vineyard is not a stack of unrelated diagrams. It is a one-parameter family of persistence diagrams realised as curves in birth–death–time space.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Vineyard modules: what the vineyard omits
text:
Vineyard modules: what the vineyard omits
A vineyard module retains more than the visible trajectories. It consists of the persistence module \(V_t\) at each external time together with coherent interleaving maps between the modules at different times. Schematically, the horizontal direction is ordinary persistence through filtration height, while the vertical direction transports information through physical time: \[\begin{array}{ccccc}
V_s(a)&\longrightarrow&V_s(b)&\longrightarrow&V_s(c)\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
V_t(a+\varepsilon)&\longrightarrow&
V_t(b+\varepsilon)&\longrightarrow&
V_t(c+\varepsilon).
\end{array}\]
▶ Likely sticking point. For a single well-behaved one-parameter module, its barcode classifies the module up to isomorphism. But the source and target barcodes do not classify a particular map between two modules. Dynamic questions may depend on those maps.
A direct sum of vine modules would mean that each visible vine can be treated as one independent algebraic feature for all time: \[I[\gamma_1]\oplus\cdots\oplus I[\gamma_m].\] Turner’s central point is that a vineyard may visibly contain several vines while its vineyard module is nevertheless indecomposable. The homology generators can mix under transport through time.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
Concrete reading of Turner Figure 1
Use Figure 1 of Turner, Representing Vineyard Modules, as the concrete example.
The domain is a disc divided into four pieces:

\(A\): the open inner disc;
\(B\): the inner boundary circle;
\(C\): the open surrounding annulus;
\(D\): the outer boundary circle.

The time-dependent function assigns \[f_t(A)=21-t,\qquad f_t(B)=14-t,\qquad
f_t(C)=15+t,\qquad f_t(D)=t.\]
◇ Object check. The horizontal axis in the figure is external time \(t\). The vertical axis is filtration height \(a\). The four black sloping lines are the values of \(f_t\) on \(A,B,C,D\). At a fixed \(t\), move vertically upward to watch the sublevel set acquire these four pieces.
The critical ordering changes when lines cross: \[f_3(A)=f_3(C),\qquad f_7(B)=f_7(D).\] Hence the dashed vertical lines at \(t=3\) and \(t=7\) divide three regimes. At every fixed time there are two \(H_1\) bars: \[[14-t,21-t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
[t,15+t).\] The coloured vertical segments drawn at selected times are these bars. Following each colour through time produces a vine.
The first bar is born when \(B\) enters and dies when \(A\) fills its inner loop. The second is born when \(D\) enters and dies when \(C\) fills the annular class.
▶ Likely sticking point. The coloured curves make the example look like two independent features, but the visible vines do not determine how their homology generators are transported through time. That missing information is exactly what the vineyard module retains.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Why the Figure 1 module is indecomposable
text:
Why the Figure 1 module is indecomposable
Before the first critical event, a natural basis is \[[B],\qquad[D+B],\] whereas after the second critical event the forced basis is \[[B],\qquad[D].\] Over \(\mathbb F_2\), \[[D]=[D+B]+[B].\] Thus the change of basis mixes the two visible vines. After coherent simplification, an off-diagonal term remains in a transport matrix of the form \[\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}.\]
The off-diagonal \(1\) means that transporting the second generator through time necessarily picks up part of the first. There is no globally coherent choice of bases that turns the family into two independent \(1\times 1\) problems.

Two visible vines do not necessarily mean two independent evolving homology classes.

This is the conceptual reason to care about persistence modules rather than only diagrams: the diagram records where classes are born and die; the module-level maps record how classes are related and transported.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
Why vineyards are delicate
Smooth motion of points does not necessarily imply smooth behaviour of the filtration order. In a moving point cloud, many distances can change relative order at once. Edges, triangles and higher-dimensional simplices can undergo large global reorderings. This makes it hard to identify the same topological feature across time. The persistence diagram may be stable in bottleneck distance, while feature identity is still unstable.
This is the distinction to emphasise: \[\text{diagram stability} \neq \text{reliable feature tracking}.\]
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Case 5: labels, colours or types matter
text:
Case 5: labels, colours or types matter
If points, regions or agents carry labels, colours or types, ordinary persistence may ignore the structure of interest. Chromatic or relative-style methods ask how different classes spatially mingle, separate or interact. Relative homology, image persistence, kernel persistence and cokernel persistence can be introduced conceptually here as tools for asking what part of a feature belongs to, is contributed by, or is shared across different subobjects.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
text:
DP relevance
For swarms or physical reservoirs, vineyards are attractive because they offer feature identity, continuous trajectories and potential online updates. But they are also high risk. A literal moving point-cloud Rips filtration may not satisfy the assumptions needed for vineyard tracking.
Two more plausible strategies are:

fix an interaction-graph or clique-complex scaffold and let edge or simplex weights vary smoothly through time;
fix an ambient mesh and define a smooth density or activity field from the swarm or reservoir state.

Both strategies disconnect the fixed simplicial object from the raw moving agent geometry. The topology then belongs to an interaction structure or ambient field rather than directly to the moving point cloud.
crumbs: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?

title: Week 8: Beyond ordinary persistence: which advanced tool solves which problem?
section: Software scope: Python first, Julia as a research extension
text:
Software scope: Python first, Julia as a research extension
The implemented course should retain Python as its primary environment. GUDHI supplies simplex-tree, Rips and cubical representations together with persistent-cohomology tools, while Ripser.py provides a focused interface for Rips persistence on point clouds and distance matrices. This covers the static, validation and repeated-persistence workflows used in Weeks 4–7.
Julia becomes attractive when the surrounding dynamical simulation or numerical workflow is already written in Julia, or when a benchmark of the pure-Julia Ripserer implementation is scientifically useful. Ripserer supports ordinary persistence computations and representative cocycle workflows. It should not be introduced merely to reproduce the same classroom barcode in a second language.
Interoperability is feasible through PythonCall/JuliaCall, including controlled conversion and non-copying array exchange. For a research prototype, prefer a narrow boundary: exchange point arrays, distance matrices or persistence intervals, rather than passing live complex objects between runtimes.
Current recommendation. Keep the reproducible teaching pipeline in Python. Add a Julia benchmark only when the DP simulation is Julia-native or when profiling identifies persistence computation as a real bottleneck. Treat zigzag, multiparameter and vineyard-module computation as separate research evaluations; ordinary Ripser interoperability does not supply those methods automatically.
Official capability references: GUDHI Python documentation, Ripser.py documentation, Ripserer.jl documentation, and PythonCall/JuliaCall.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
text:
This is the worked example for live teaching. It follows the conceptual sequence of the Week 1 slides and makes each computational claim visible. It is not an answer key to every practical choice.
Resource boundary. The reference notes explain the ideas fully. The slides carry the visual argument. This notebook supplies the lecturer’s prediction-and-reveal sequence. The participant practical asks students to make their own descriptor, threshold and interpretation choices.
Lecture map. First reveal the 13 Datasaurus clouds after their matching summaries. Then compare geometric descriptors, test which transformations retain distances, and finally keep the observations fixed while changing a graph threshold. The conclusion is about selective summaries and constructed representations, not yet persistent homology.
Suggested rhythm: show the slide, ask for a prediction, then reveal the corresponding notebook output.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
text:
Demonstration setup
The helper functions keep the machinery visible: whitening, pairwise distances, threshold adjacency, component search and the graph identity \(E-V+C\). No TDA library is called.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RNG = np.random.default_rng(3024)

def standardise_shape(points):
    """Centre and whiten a two-dimensional point cloud."""
    centred = np.asarray(points, dtype=float) - np.mean(points, axis=0)
    covariance = np.cov(centred, rowvar=False)
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariance)
    return centred @ vectors @ np.diag(values ** -0.5)

def scalar_summary(points):
    return {
        'mean_x': np.mean(points[:, 0]),
        'mean_y': np.mean(points[:, 1]),
        'sd_x': np.std(points[:, 0], ddof=1),
        'sd_y': np.std(points[:, 1], ddof=1),
        'correlation': np.corrcoef(points.T)[0, 1],
    }

def pairwise_distances(points):
    differences = points[:, None, :] - points[None, :, :]
    return np.sqrt(np.sum(differences ** 2, axis=2))

def threshold_graph_statistics(points, epsilon):
    """Return V, E, components and graph cycle rank at one threshold."""
    distances = pairwise_distances(points)
    adjacency = (distances <= epsilon) & (distances > 0)
    vertices = len(points)
    edges = int(np.sum(adjacency) // 2)
    unseen = set(range(vertices))
    components = 0
    while unseen:
        components += 1
        stack = [unseen.pop()]
        while stack:
            vertex = stack.pop()
            neighbours = set(np.flatnonzero(adjacency[vertex])) & unseen
            unseen -= neighbours
            stack.extend(neighbours)
    cycle_rank = edges - vertices + components
    return {'vertices': vertices, 'edges': edges,
            'components': components, 'graph_cycle_rank': cycle_rank}

print('Environment ready. Random seed: 3024')

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
section: Demonstration 1, after slide “Matching moments, different organisation”
text:
Demonstration 1, after slide “Matching moments, different organisation”
Ask before running: If 13 clouds have nearly identical coordinate means, standard deviations and correlations, how different could their organisation be? What evidence do your eyes use to distinguish them?
Demonstration 1 uses the canonical 1,846-row Datasaurus Dozen CSV. Reveal the table of coordinate moments and correlations first, then reveal the 13 scatter plots.


Code
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def find_datasaurus_csv():
    candidates = [
        Path('datasaurus_dozen.csv'),
        Path('data/datasaurus_dozen.csv'),
        Path('../../data/datasaurus_dozen.csv'),
    ]
    for candidate in candidates:
        if candidate.exists():
            return candidate
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        'Download datasaurus_dozen.csv from the Week 1 page and place it '
        'beside this notebook.'
    )

datasaurus_path = find_datasaurus_csv()
datasaurus = pd.read_csv(datasaurus_path)
dataset_order = list(datasaurus['dataset'].drop_duplicates())

groups = datasaurus.groupby('dataset', sort=False)
summaries = groups.agg(
    n=('x', 'size'),
    mean_x=('x', 'mean'),
    mean_y=('y', 'mean'),
    sd_x=('x', 'std'),
    sd_y=('y', 'std'),
)
summaries['correlation'] = [group['x'].corr(group['y']) for _, group in groups]
print(summaries.round(3).to_string())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 4, figsize=(10, 10), sharex=True, sharey=True,
                         constrained_layout=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, dataset_order):
    group = datasaurus[datasaurus['dataset'] == name]
    ax.scatter(group['x'], group['y'], s=10)
    ax.set_title(name.replace('_', ' '))
    ax.set_aspect('equal', adjustable='box')
    ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
for ax in axes.flat[len(dataset_order):]:
    ax.axis('off')
fig.supxlabel('x'); fig.supylabel('y')
plt.show()

# A few transparent geometric questions, still without topology.
def convex_hull(points):
    ordered = sorted(set(map(tuple, points)))
    def cross(o, a, b):
        return (a[0] - o[0]) * (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) * (b[0] - o[0])
    lower, upper = [], []
    for point in ordered:
        while len(lower) >= 2 and cross(lower[-2], lower[-1], point) <= 0:
            lower.pop()
        lower.append(point)
    for point in reversed(ordered):
        while len(upper) >= 2 and cross(upper[-2], upper[-1], point) <= 0:
            upper.pop()
        upper.append(point)
    return np.asarray(lower[:-1] + upper[:-1])

def geometric_descriptors(points):
    distances = pairwise_distances(points)
    np.fill_diagonal(distances, np.inf)
    hull = convex_hull(points)
    area = 0.5 * abs(np.dot(hull[:, 0], np.roll(hull[:, 1], 1))
                     - np.dot(hull[:, 1], np.roll(hull[:, 0], 1)))
    radii = np.linalg.norm(points - points.mean(axis=0), axis=1)
    eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.cov(points.T))
    return {
        'median nearest distance': np.median(distances.min(axis=1)),
        'convex-hull area': area,
        'radial coefficient of variation': radii.std() / radii.mean(),
        'covariance anisotropy': eigenvalues[-1] / eigenvalues[0],
    }

worked_names = ['circle', 'bullseye', 'dots', 'dino']
worked_geometry = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, worked_names):
    points = datasaurus.loc[datasaurus['dataset'] == name, ['x', 'y']].to_numpy()
    worked_geometry[name] = geometric_descriptors(points)
    hull = convex_hull(points)
    closed_hull = np.vstack((hull, hull[0]))
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], s=9)
    ax.plot(closed_hull[:, 0], closed_hull[:, 1], color='tab:orange', linewidth=1.3)
    ax.set(title=name, xlim=(0, 100), ylim=(0, 100), aspect='equal')
plt.show()
display(pd.DataFrame(worked_geometry).T.round(3))

# Retain one canonical circle for the controlled transformation section.
ring_raw = datasaurus.loc[datasaurus['dataset'] == 'circle', ['x', 'y']].to_numpy()
ring = standardise_shape(ring_raw)



Teaching point: visual intuition is doing real work
The 13 groups have nearly equal coordinate means, coordinate standard deviations and Pearson correlations, but differ radically in point arrangement. Matejka and Fitzmaurice constructed the datasets through simulated annealing to preserve those numerical values while changing the plotted form. The example motivates richer questions; it does not show that geometry has failed or that topology is always the right description.
First ask the room to contrast circle, bullseye, dots, star and dino. Collect the visual cues before naming methods: local density, spacing, direction, curvature, boundary, symmetry, clusters, branches, empty regions and scale. Visual judgement combines far more spatial information than the table of coordinate means, coordinate standard deviations and Pearson correlations.
Then separate four questions:

Global summaries: where is the cloud centred and how do coordinates co-vary?
Richer geometry: how far apart, dense, curved, directed or symmetric are the observations? A nearest-neighbour distribution, convex hull, density estimate or full distance matrix can distinguish point arrangements that coordinate means, coordinate standard deviations and Pearson correlation cannot distinguish.
Topology and homology: after constructing a space, how is it connected and which holes occur? Exact lengths and curvature are deliberately ignored.
Persistent topology: when do selected homological features appear and disappear as the construction scale changes?

Use circle versus ellipse for different geometry but the same topology; circle versus figure eight for different loop structure; and ring boundary versus filled disk for a hole versus no hole. Note that homology is coarse: equal Betti numbers do not imply homeomorphism.
Keep interpretations of the Datasaurus plots provisional. A visible white region is not yet a homology class, and ordinary homology does not completely describe branching. Demonstrations 3 to 5 introduce neighbourhood graphs and scale dependence. Weeks 2 to 4 supply simplicial complexes, homology and persistence. Demonstration 2 uses the canonical circle dataset for a controlled transformation comparison.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
section: Demonstration 2, after slides “Geometry and topology” and “The rubber-sheet idea”
text:
Demonstration 2, after slides “Geometry and topology” and “The rubber-sheet idea”
Ask before running: Which transformations preserve the pairwise distance matrix? Which preserve the topology of the underlying continuous circle?
Translation and rotation are Euclidean isometries. The anisotropic stretch is still an invertible continuous deformation, but is not an isometry.


Code
angle = np.deg2rad(35)
rotation = np.array([[np.cos(angle), -np.sin(angle)],
                     [np.sin(angle),  np.cos(angle)]])
transformed = {
    'original': ring,
    'translated': ring + np.array([3.0, -1.5]),
    'rotated': ring @ rotation.T,
    'anisotropically stretched': ring @ np.diag([1.8, 0.55]),
}

baseline = pairwise_distances(ring)
for name, points in transformed.items():
    change = np.max(np.abs(pairwise_distances(points) - baseline))
    print(f'{name:26s} maximum distance change = {change:.3f}')



Teaching point
All three transformed continuous rings are homeomorphic to the original circle. Only translation and rotation leave every Euclidean pairwise distance unchanged. A construction based on one fixed metric threshold can therefore change under a homeomorphism.
▶ Likely sticking point. Topological invariance of an underlying continuous space does not make every data-derived metric construction invariant.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
section: Demonstration 3, after slide “Finite data do not arrive with a hole label”
text:
Demonstration 3, after slide “Finite data do not arrive with a hole label”
The noisy ring and disk are finite samples. Neither comes labelled with the topology of a latent space.
Ask before running: What modelling object could we build using only pairwise distances, and which choice would it require?


Code
n_noisy = 90
angles = RNG.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_noisy)
noisy_ring = np.column_stack((np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)))
noisy_ring += RNG.normal(0, 0.055, size=(n_noisy, 2))

disk_radii = np.sqrt(RNG.uniform(0, 1, n_noisy))
disk_angles = RNG.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_noisy)
noisy_disk = np.column_stack((disk_radii * np.cos(disk_angles),
                              disk_radii * np.sin(disk_angles)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.5, 3.7), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (name, points) in zip(axes, [('noisy ring', noisy_ring),
                                     ('filled disk sample', noisy_disk)]):
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], s=18)
    ax.set(title=name, aspect='equal', xlim=(-1.2, 1.2), ylim=(-1.2, 1.2))
plt.show()

section: Demonstration 4, alongside slide “A first transparent diagnostic”
text:
Demonstration 4, alongside slide “A first transparent diagnostic”
At threshold \(\varepsilon\), join points at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). For this graph,
\[\text{cycle rank}=E-V+C.\]
Ask before running: As \(\varepsilon\) increases, should components and graph cycle rank move in the same direction?


Code
epsilons = np.linspace(0.08, 0.65, 24)
results = {}
for name, points in [('noisy ring', noisy_ring), ('disk sample', noisy_disk)]:
    results[name] = [threshold_graph_statistics(points, epsilon)
                     for epsilon in epsilons]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.7), constrained_layout=True)
for name, records in results.items():
    axes[0].plot(epsilons, [r['components'] for r in records], label=name)
    axes[1].plot(epsilons, [r['graph_cycle_rank'] for r in records], label=name)
axes[0].set(xlabel=r'threshold $\varepsilon$', ylabel='connected components')
axes[1].set(xlabel=r'threshold $\varepsilon$', ylabel=r'graph cycle rank $E-V+C$')
for ax in axes:
    ax.legend()
plt.show()

chosen_epsilon = 0.28
for name, points in [('noisy ring', noisy_ring), ('disk sample', noisy_disk)]:
    print(name, threshold_graph_statistics(points, chosen_epsilon))



Reveal and pause
At small thresholds both graphs fragment. Components merge as the threshold grows. Graph cycle rank can then grow rapidly because new edges create graph cycles.
The rapid growth in graph cycle rank is the point at which to separate the threshold graph from its clique complex. Filled triangles would turn many three-edge graph cycles into boundaries, so the plotted graph-cycle-rank curve is not a curve of first Betti numbers for the full Rips complex.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
section: Demonstration 5, alongside slide “One threshold is a modelling choice”
text:
Demonstration 5, alongside slide “One threshold is a modelling choice”
Use three thresholds on exactly the same observations. The point is not to select a winner. It is to reveal how strongly a conclusion can depend on one threshold.


Code
for epsilon in [0.16, 0.28, 0.48]:
    print(f'epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}')
    for name, points in [('noisy ring', noisy_ring), ('disk sample', noisy_disk)]:
        print(' ', name, threshold_graph_statistics(points, epsilon))



Teaching point
One threshold produces one constructed graph and one answer. A sweep makes the scale dependence visible, but graph cycle rank still belongs to a graph rather than to the filled simplicial complexes introduced in Week 2. The lesson here is that the representation and threshold are part of the result.

title: Week 1 lecture walkthrough: from matching summaries to constructed shape
section: Close the lecture: what has and has not been established
text:
Close the lecture: what has and has not been established

Matching means, standard deviations and correlation do not imply matching spatial organisation.
The observed coordinates, distance rule, threshold graph and any later complex are distinct objects.
Homeomorphic continuous shapes need not have identical metric constructions at a fixed threshold.
Graph cycle rank is not generally \(H_1\) of the clique complex.
Sweeping a threshold reveals sensitivity, but it does not by itself define simplicial homology.

Return to the slide “Before we leave” and ask the class to name one choice at every arrow:
\[\text{data}\to\text{representation}\to\text{metric}\to\text{complex}\to\text{summary}.\]

\[

\to\text{state-space point cloud}.
\]
